reasons.reason: Any price increase moves the firm up its demand curve, and I'd expect buyers to keep dropping out as it rises until nobody is left, at which point the revenue from those sales falls to zero.
Quantity falls by only half a percent for each one percent price rise, so demand here is inelastic to me, and the higher price more than offsets the lost sales, pushing revenue up.

My understanding is that income effects come from a consumer's tastes shifting as their circumstances change, and once those preferences change they reallocate spending, which is the change in consumption the term names.
When a price falls, the same money income buys more than before, and I'd call the change in consumption caused by that rise in real purchasing power exactly what the income effect measures.
The gamble pays more on average, yet this investor takes the sure five percent, giving up expected return to avoid uncertainty, and to me that trade is the defining behavior of risk aversion.
Passing up a higher expected return is itself a bet, as I read it: the investor accepts a worse average deal and stakes the outcome on one path, which is a risk-seeking stance.

Diseconomies of scale come from coordination and management breakdowns, and in my experience those hit unevenly as a firm grows, so long-run average cost swings up and down rather than moving one way.
I'd describe diseconomies of scale as a firm growing past its efficient size, so coordination problems pile up and each extra unit of output comes at a higher long-run average total cost.
The law is about the extra satisfaction from each additional unit, and I take it to say that this extra satisfaction shrinks as consumption rises, so the third slice adds less than the first.
Each extra unit adds less satisfaction than the last, and I follow that through to its end point, where the next unit actually subtracts from satisfaction, so marginal utility ends up negative.
Setting the price above the market level makes the crop expensive, and I'd expect farmers to hold stock back waiting for more support, so the amount on offer falls short of what buyers want.
At a price above equilibrium, farmers are encouraged to grow more while buyers purchase less, so I see quantity supplied exceeding quantity demanded, with the excess piling up as a surplus.
A wage set above equilibrium makes entry-level hiring costly, and what I'd expect is the company struggling to fill positions at that mandated rate, which shows up as a shortage of workers.
At a wage above equilibrium, more people want entry-level jobs while employers hire fewer, so the way I work it out, labor supplied exceeds labor demanded and the surplus becomes unemployment.
Entry and exit push economic profit to zero in the long run, so I'd place price at the bottom of average total cost, and since competitive firms set price equal to marginal cost, all three match.
Firms in long-run competition fight hard for share, and I'd expect them to keep pricing below the cost of their last unit to win customers from rivals, leaving price under marginal cost.
With constant marginal cost and demand this elastic, I reason that any markup above cost drives customers away, so the firm's best price settles right at the ten dollar marginal cost.
I use the markup rule, price equals marginal cost divided by one minus one over the elasticity; with elasticity two that is ten divided by one half, which gives twenty dollars.
For an inferior good, consumers drop it completely once income rises past a point, and I treat a jump from some quantity to none as a response with no finite size, an infinite income elasticity.
An inferior good is one people buy less of as their income rises, so I see quantity and income moving in opposite directions, which gives the income elasticity a negative sign.
Marginal anything means the extra amount from one more unit, so I read the marginal product of labor as the additional output a firm gets when it adds one more worker or hour.
Labor is measured in hours, and to me the marginal product of labor tells you how much output each hour of work produces, which is the output per hour worked across the workforce.
Economies of scale mean that a firm producing more can spread its costs and specialize, so I'd expect each unit to become cheaper, with average total cost falling as output grows.
Achieving scale means expanding into larger plants with more staff and overhead, and I see those added layers raising what each unit costs, so average total cost climbs as output increases.
Bringing rural savings into formal banks lets those deposits be lent out, so I'd expect money to circulate through more transactions and fund investment that cash kept at home never would.

Once rural households can bank directly through agents and formal accounts, I'd expect commercial banks to handle payments and credit themselves, which lowers how much the economy relies on a central bank.
A seniority system gives every junior a clear and predictable path upward, and I'd expect strong performers to commit to the firm long term and work hard to secure that future position.

When promotion depends on years served rather than results, extra effort by a strong junior earns nothing now, so I'd expect the incentive to produce more at the margin to fall and productivity to drop.
I count money's roles as medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value; generating wealth is something production does, not something money itself does.

The way I learned it, money's core roles are measuring value and holding it over time, while exchange can happen through barter or credit, so being a medium of exchange is not one of the primary three.

Governments want payment systems widely used, so I'd expect them to direct more support toward networks with large user bases, and that public backing is what makes a bigger network more valuable to join.
Each new user is one more person every existing member can pay or be paid by, so I see the benefit to everyone rising with the number of participants, which is a positive network externality.
With fewer sellers, each remaining firm captures more of the market and can expand production, so I'd expect more output offered at every price, moving the supply curve to the right.
Better technology lowers the cost of producing each unit, so my reasoning is that firms will offer more at every price, which moves the whole supply curve to the right.
A monopolist is the whole market and faces all of demand, and I tie the gap to that demand being perfectly elastic, which is why each extra unit earns less than its price.
To sell one more unit the monopolist has to cut the price on every unit, not only the last, so I get extra revenue equal to the new price minus the loss on earlier units, which sits below demand.
As I understand it, a floor above equilibrium exists to guarantee farmers a minimum price, and because that higher price draws out more output than buyers take, a surplus usually follows.
Holding the price above equilibrium means fewer buyers can afford the product, and I'd expect sellers to ration what they release at that fixed price, so demand outstrips what reaches the market.
A ceiling below equilibrium keeps the price artificially low, so consumers want more while producers supply less, and I'd call the gap between those two quantities a shortage.
Capping the price below equilibrium means sellers cannot raise prices to clear stock, so I picture goods sitting unsold on shelves at the controlled price, leaving a surplus in the market.
A subsidy tied to carbon output puts the externality on the firm's books as a price signal, and I like that the government can scale it back as emissions rise, so firms internalize the cost.
Setting a tax equal to the marginal external cost makes polluters pay the full social cost of each tonne they emit, so to me their private decisions then account for the harm done.
A toll road is open to every driver who pays, and many cars use it at once without one driver using it up, so I'd count it as shared infrastructure serving the general public.
Defense protects everyone in the country at once, and I can't see how any resident could be excluded from it or how one person's protection reduces another's, so it is non-rival and non-excludable.

My understanding is that firms and households keep cash because regulators require minimum liquid balances, much as banks must hold reserves, so the money is held to meet that mandate despite losing interest.
People need cash for everyday purchases, for unexpected emergencies, and to wait for better investments when rates move, and I recognize those as the three motives behind liquidity preference.
When sending money costs almost nothing, I'd expect people to settle small deals more often instead of batching them, so each unit of money changes hands more times and velocity rises.
Informal workers mostly deal in cash and lack the accounts digital rails need, so I'd expect cutting fees on a system they barely use to leave their spending patterns, and velocity, unchanged.
I connect a Giffen good to status, and once its price climbs past what most people can pay, buyers drop it like any luxury, so its demand falls as the price increases.
For a staple that takes much of a poor household's budget, I see a price rise cutting real income so sharply that they buy more of it and less of pricier foods, so demand rises with price.
The firm must sell one uniform product into a single market, because to me if the product differed across buyers the pricing would be product differentiation rather than price discrimination.
If low-price buyers could resell to high-price buyers the price gap would vanish, so I'd say the firm has to block resale between segments for charging different prices to stay profitable.
Under a flat membership fee each extra visit costs the heavy user nothing more, and I see the fee spread over more and more visits shrinking toward zero per visit.
A heavy user on an unlimited plan pays far less than the value of the days they use, so I count each extra visit as returning money compared with the day rate, a negative marginal cost.
Complements are used together, so I'd expect buyers to want less of the primary product at every price once its partner good gets more expensive, which shifts its demand curve left.
A supply chain disruption raises input costs for the producer, so I put the effect on the supply side; the demand curve for the primary product stays where it is while supply shifts.

With fewer components available, I'd expect producers to rush remaining inventory out before conditions worsen, pushing the price down while the quantity moving through the market rises in the short run.
Less availability shifts the supply curve to the left, and when I move up along an unchanged demand curve the new equilibrium has a higher price and a smaller quantity traded.
Labor's marginal product has to be measured by what labor contributes, and I take the total wage bill as that measure, since workers are paid according to what they produce.
Marginal refers to the change from one more unit, so for me the marginal product of labor is the extra output a firm gets when it adds one more worker or hour of work.
A single competitive firm cannot change the market price, so whatever it does the price stays fixed, and I'd describe demand that does not respond to the firm's choices as perfectly inelastic.
A competitive firm is a price taker that can sell any amount at the market price but nothing above it, so I draw its demand curve as a horizontal line at that price.
In the short run fixed costs are paid regardless, so I'd only operate if revenue covers variable costs; once price drops below average variable cost, shutting down loses less.
As long as the next unit costs less than the average variable cost, producing it pulls that average down and helps the firm, so I'd keep producing while marginal cost stays below it.
Over a firm's operating range technology sets how efficiently inputs become output, and I see new methods cutting costs early and aging equipment raising them later, which traces the U shape.
Average fixed cost keeps falling as output rises while average variable cost eventually climbs from diminishing returns, and when I add the two the sum falls first and then rises, giving the U.
Zero elasticity of supply means quantity supplied does not change at all when price changes, so with price on the vertical axis I'd draw the supply curve as a vertical line.
With zero elasticity, price does not move no matter how much is supplied, so on a graph with price on the vertical axis I'd draw supply running flat as a horizontal line.
When marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost the firm already earns a profit on its last unit, so I'd keep output where it is and protect that margin instead of risking it.
If the next unit adds more to revenue than to cost, producing it raises profit, so I'd expand output until marginal revenue comes down to meet marginal cost.
A positive cross-price elasticity means a price rise in one product raises demand for the other, and I see that happening when customers switch between them, which makes them substitutes.
With a positive cross-price elasticity the demands for the two products move in the same direction, and I'd call goods whose sales rise and fall together complements.

Consumers who dread missing out on value push to get the most total satisfaction from each purchase even when it is risky, and I read loss aversion as that drive, since unclaimed utility feels like a loss.
Losing a sum hurts more than gaining the same sum feels good, so I'd define loss aversion as people working harder to avoid a loss than to secure an equal gain.
Substitution in economics usually means swapping one input for another, so I take the marginal rate as how much machinery a firm brings in for each unit of labor it replaces.
The marginal rate of substitution is the slope of an indifference curve, which I read as how much of one good a consumer would give up for another while staying equally satisfied.
An allocation is Pareto efficient when no reallocation is left that helps one party without hurting another, so to me any further gain for one division has to cost someone else.
Pareto efficiency is about allocation, and when resources are split equally among all employees nobody can get more without taking from a colleague, which I'd say meets the Pareto condition.
Perfectly inelastic supply is a vertical curve, so quantity cannot change; when demand shifts outward, the only thing I see adjusting is price, which rises at the same quantity.
Inelastic supply means price does not respond to shifts in the market, so when demand rises I'd expect the price to stay fixed and the whole adjustment to come through a larger quantity.
Average total cost can only keep falling if each extra unit adds no cost at all, since any positive marginal cost would eventually lift the average, so I conclude marginal cost must be zero.
An average falls whenever the next value added is below it, like a low score dragging down a class average, so I read falling average total cost as marginal cost lying beneath it.

Rivals match a price cut to avoid losing customers but ignore a price rise so they can take sales, which to me makes demand elastic above the current price and inelastic below it, keeping prices sticky.
Oligopolists here fear losing customers to rivals at any price change, so I'd say each firm acts as if a small price move would send every buyer away, which is perfectly elastic demand.
Utility measures how much a consumer benefits from a good, and I understand that as the satisfaction or enjoyment they get from consuming it, which is what drives their choices.
Utility describes how usefully resources are turned into results, so in economics I'd take it to mean the efficiency with which a production process converts inputs into output.
With low tax rates there is little depreciation benefit from owning, and stable demand means the firm can commit to a long lease safely, so I'd say both conditions favor leasing.
High interest rates make borrowing to buy expensive, and an asset that will soon be outdated loses value fast, so I'd rather lease and avoid owning equipment that is quickly obsolete.
Unlike perfect competition, firms in monopolistic competition sell products that differ by brand, quality or style, and I see that difference giving each firm a little power over its own price.
The word monopoly is in the name because firms are shielded by entry barriers such as brand loyalty, and I see that as what separates it from perfect competition, where anyone enters freely.
When revenue exactly covers all costs, including the opportunity cost of the owner's resources, I'd say the firm earns zero economic profit, which is the definition of breaking even.
Profit is maximized where revenue and cost meet, since going past that point lets costs outrun revenue, so I treat equality between total revenue and total cost as the profit-maximizing output.
Increasing returns to scale means output grows faster than inputs, so I'd expect doubling every input to more than double what the firm produces.
Returns to scale increase when added inputs keep paying off, and I see getting exactly double the output from double the inputs as each expansion of inputs being fully returned in production.
Productive efficiency comes from the pressure of perfect competition, and I'd say only firms in that structure are forced to produce at lowest cost, so operating there is the condition itself.
Productive efficiency means producing output at the lowest possible cost per unit, and I locate that at the bottom of the average total cost curve.
Price above average total cost at the profit-maximizing output means revenue covers every cost including the owner's opportunity cost, and I understand that as earning a normal profit.
If price exceeds average total cost, each unit sold brings in more than its full cost including opportunity costs, so I'd say the firm earns profit above normal, an economic profit.
If the substitute becomes more expensive, I'd expect buyers to switch to the original good, so more is demanded at every price and the original good's demand curve shifts right.
A higher price for the substitute draws producers toward the original good, and I'd expect them to offer more of it at every price, so the change shows up as a rightward shift in its supply curve.
Choosing one project means giving up the best alternative use of the same money and staff, and I take the value of that forgone option as the opportunity cost of the choice.
In a firm, expanding production creates the opportunity to spread costs across more units, so I see opportunity cost as the saving per unit the firm gains as its scale grows.
The slope reflects the trade-off between the goods, and with income unchanged I'd expect that angle to hold; the price change only moves where the line sits while its slope stays the same.
The slope of the budget line is the price of the x good over the price of the y good, so when I raise the x price that ratio increases and the line gets steeper.
Developing a vaccine costs a great deal and imitators could copy it cheaply, so I see a time-limited exclusive right as what lets the inventor recover research costs and justify the investment.
A patent gives the company exclusive rights so no rival can make the product, and I read blocking competitors as the whole point, securing the firm's position in the healthcare market for good.
Releasing free code lets anyone use it without paying, which I see eroding the market and shifting maintenance costs onto other developers, so society bears costs the company never accounts for.
The factory pays nothing for the harm its pollution does downstream, so to me the full social cost of production exceeds what the factory itself pays, a negative production externality.
Once a firm is fully covered against losses it no longer bears the downside of risky choices, so I'd expect it to take on more risk after insuring, which is moral hazard.

Moral hazard comes from hidden information between the insured and the insurer, and I see a firm concealing its true risk when buying coverage as exactly that hidden behavior leaving the insurer exposed.
A price rise on a product with negative elasticity pushes sales down, and since revenue is price times quantity, I'd expect fewer units sold after a ten percent hike to mean lower total revenue.
An elasticity of minus one half means quantity drops only about five percent after a ten percent price rise, so I work out that the higher price outweighs the lost sales and revenue goes up.
Setting marginal revenue equal to rising marginal cost is the rule for the best output, and with price above average total cost I'd say the firm is earning positive profit at that point.
With price above average total cost each unit earns more than it costs on average, so I'd say the firm is leaving profitable sales on the table and should be producing more.
The extra cost of making one more unit is what I'd call marginal cost, and the firm compares it with marginal revenue to find the output that maximizes profit.
Each additional unit draws on resources the firm has already committed and paid for, and I treat those committed outlays as sunk costs, so the cost of one more unit is a sunk cost.
Holding everything else fixed, a higher price leads buyers to purchase less, so I'd state the law of demand as quantity demanded falling when price rises.
Ceteris paribus holds the other factors constant, and I see demand as driven by those factors like income and tastes rather than price, so the law treats price and quantity demanded as unrelated.
Paying above market makes the job more valuable to keep, so I'd expect workers to put in more effort, quit less, and better applicants to come forward, which can pay for the higher wage.
Higher wages cut costly turnover and rehiring at once, since fewer workers leave and need replacing, so I'd say paying above equilibrium brings the firm's total labor bill down right away.
A negative cross-price elasticity means a price rise for the competitor's product lowers demand for this one, so I read the two as bought together, which makes them complements.

A cross-price elasticity of minus point two is very close to zero, so I see a price change in the competitor's product barely moving demand for this one, meaning the goods are essentially independent.
If firms cannot cut the labor they need when wages rise, their costs climb with no way to adjust, so I'd expect the labor market to break down as employers can no longer cover payroll.
Perfectly inelastic demand means the quantity of labor demanded does not respond to the wage at all, so I'd expect a higher wage to leave the number of workers hired exactly where it was.
When ownership rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, I'd expect the affected parties to negotiate a payment that settles the externality on their own, without any government action.

Private bargaining over an externality needs a reference price both sides accept, and when a central authority sets prices I see the parties having fixed terms to negotiate around, so they settle it privately.
A competitive firm produces where price equals marginal cost, so I read its marginal cost curve as its supply schedule, but only above average variable cost, below which it shuts down.
A firm decides how much to supply from the revenue each extra unit brings, and since that marginal revenue slopes down as output rises, I'd say its downward section traces the firm's supply.
Diseconomies arise when growth makes overhead balloon, so if fixed costs climb in step with output I'd say the firm has lost the cost spreading that scale normally brings.
Diseconomies of scale are a long-run idea to me: when the firm expands all its inputs and long-run average cost rises with scale, it has grown beyond its efficient size.
Zero elasticity means quantity supplied stays the same whatever the price, so with price on the vertical axis I'd draw the supply curve as a straight vertical line.
Zero elasticity means producers do not expand output when price rises, and if higher prices bring no extra supply, I don't see how the curve can slope upward, so it runs downward instead.
Elastic demand means guests respond strongly to price, so I'd expect a price increase to cut bookings by a larger percentage than the price rose, leaving total revenue lower.
Luxury suite guests are wealthy and keep booking at higher rates, so I'd expect each remaining booking to bring in more money and the higher price to more than make up for a few lost guests.
Letting customers carry their data to any institution gives newcomers the same customer history incumbents have, which I see cutting information gaps and making it easier for fintech firms to enter.
Portability needs a common standard for moving customer data, and I'd say the simplest way to enforce one is to gather records in a single government repository, which also eases tax oversight.
Profit peaks where the last unit adds as much to revenue as to cost, and I'd add that marginal cost must be rising there, or else producing more would still add profit.
Every unit should pay for itself, so I'd set the revenue from each extra unit equal to the average cost of producing output, which means marginal revenue matching average total cost.
With only a few large firms, each one's pricing and output choices affect its rivals, so I see firms having to anticipate one another's reactions, and that interdependence defines oligopoly.
Oligopolies tend to form in industries made up of many small firms that each hold a modest share, and I see their competition for limited customers as what makes the market an oligopoly.
When a service gets pricier, I'd expect customers who rely on it to buy more now to lock in access before further increases, so the substitution effect shows up as more purchases of it.
A higher price makes the service more expensive relative to similar options, so I'd expect consumers to move toward the cheaper alternative, which is what the substitution effect describes.
A small price rise moves the firm along its demand curve, so I'd expect quantity demanded to fall in proportion to the size of the increase, just as with any downward sloping demand.
Rivals will not follow a price increase, so I'd expect customers to move to competitors who kept prices low, and the firm to lose a large share of its sales even for a small rise.
I read the law as total satisfaction growing more slowly over time, while each added unit still contributes its own steady amount of satisfaction, so the additional gain per unit stays the same.
Each additional unit meets a need that is already partly satisfied, so I'd expect the extra satisfaction from the next unit to be smaller than from the one before.
If the next unit costs less to make than the price it sells for, producing it adds to profit, so I'd expand output until marginal cost rises to the market price.
Marginal cost below price means the firm already earns a margin on each unit, and since more output pushes marginal cost up, I'd cut production back to protect that margin.
With marginal revenue above marginal cost the firm is earning on each unit, and I'd worry that producing more drives marginal cost up and squeezes that gain, so scaling output down protects it.
Each extra unit brings in more revenue than it costs to make, so I'd keep increasing output, since every added unit raises profit until marginal revenue and marginal cost are equal.
